title: Strided prefetch / multi-pass attention scan notes
body:
Context: quick working notes from a small spike investigating an unexplained p99 jitter observed in production when we switched a hot route to the new paged-attention + fused-op build. This doc captures microbench runs, kernel traces, hypotheses, and short experiments to reproduce and mitigate.

Summary of findings (short):
- Observed multi-modal tail latencies due to occasional multi-pass rewalks of the attention input when strided prefetch heuristics miss alignment (common for short variable sequences with high variance).
- FlashAttention kernels are fast for the steady-state path, but fused-op helper kernels (reorder/quantize, partial-reduction) introduce microstutters when they are scheduled on the same stream and contend for L2/SM resources.
- Paged-attention page flips (memory-resident page->device) are rare but expensive; these correlate with KV cache refill traffic spikes.

Test harness & methodology:
- HW: p4d.24xlarge equivalent. CUDA 12.x, cut of runtime branch 'paged-prefetch-experiments'.
- Model: 7B transformer, seq_len distribution: 16 (40%), 64 (30%), 256 (20%), 1024 (10%).
- Workload: synthetic replay of production traces (200k requests) with preserved sequence length histogram.
- Metrics collected: per-request latency (p50/p90/p99/p999), kernel timelines via nvtx + nsight system captures, GPU SM occupancy, L2 traffic, PCIe throughput, stream concurrency counts.
- Baseline: fused-op disabled, vanilla FlashAttention.

Key microbench results (representative):
- Baseline p99: 38ms, new build p99: 62ms (same p50 ~ 9ms).
- Tail events clustered (observed via timeline) at two hotspots: (A) additional device memory loads for pageable KV segments (~120-200ms extra if page-in), (B) short 2-4ms stalls caused by fused-op helper kernels that run on the same stream as the main attention kernel leading to poor overlap.

Trace excerpts (high level):
- Case A: nvtx traces show host->device memcpy triggered mid-token for a request, followed by kernel wait. Correlates with CPU-side eviction of a rarely-used slab that paged out.
- Case B: attention kernel launches, then a reorder/quantize kernel (fused helper) issues and blocks because it uses a blocking sync call to update a shared scratch buffer. This causes subsequent token steps to wait; observed only for small batches (batch_size=1) where scheduling is more serialized.

Hypotheses:
1) Prefetch stride heuristic currently tuned for uniform sequences; sequences with alternating short and long tokens cause the prefetch to miss leading to extra device transfer.
2) Fused-op helpers are not pinned to a separate stream or priority and are performing synchronous ops that could be deferred or overlapped.
3) Small-batch degenerate scheduling prevents the runtime's intended overlap between KV copy and compute.

Experiments run (short):
- E1: force prefetch aggressive for small seqs -> reduced page-in events by 75% but increased average device memory pressure; p99 improved to 45ms but p50 degraded by ~7%.
- E2: move fused-op helpers to low-priority stream with explicit cudaStreamWaitEvent syncs -> tail events reduced; observed ~20% drop in p99. Some regressions in throughput under heavy concurrent traffic.
- E3: batched coalescer threshold adjustment (coalesce batches >=2) -> fewer serialized helper calls, p99 improved modestly for synthetic trace.

Quick recommendations (workable, short term):
- Pin fused-op helpers to a separate compute stream and ensure they use non-blocking buffer updates; only sync with the main stream at token boundary when strictly necessary.
- Increase prefetch aggressiveness for customers/routes with high seq_len variance (configurable). Add a safety cap to avoid OOM.
- Add a lightweight in-runtime sampler to detect when page-ins occur and trigger a proactive fetch for that slab for the next N requests.

Longer-term investigations:
- Kernel-level rewrite: explore merging helper logic into the main attention kernel for single-pass when sequence lengths are small to avoid separate launch overheads. Tradeoffs: code complexity vs. reduced latency spikes.
- KV cache residency policy: smarter LRU that considers upcoming trace patterns; integration with workload-aware routing (prefer instances with warmed slabs).
- Explore unified stream scheduling with stream priorities to keep critical-path kernels high priority and background helper kernels low.

Open questions:
- What % of customers will accept slightly higher average latency for much better tail behavior? Need product input (cc: Priya).
- Are there safety concerns with more aggressive prefetch for private deployments with memory caps? This should be gated in config.

Action items (owners & short timeline):
- Ethan: prototype fused-op on separate stream + non-blocking updates, test against 1M synthetic requests (due 2024-11-27).
- Priya: collect route usage patterns and identify top 10 routes with highest seq variance (due 2024-11-25).
- Marina: add in-runtime page-in telemetry flag and create a lightweight alert for production (due 2024-11-22).

Notes to self / random observations:
- Small-batch behavior is the riskiest. Many of our customers use single-request sync calls via SDK by default; consider changing SDK default to allow tiny buffering (0.05s) to permit better coalescing.
- Observed a rare kernel assert when we moved helper ops to peer-to-peer copies; file a bug if reproduced (GH PR referenced above).

Appendix: useful commands and snippets used in the spike:
- capture: nvprof/nvtx + nsight (capture cmd omitted for brevity).
- microbench snippet: python tools/bench/run_trace.py --trace data/prod-replay-2024-10-01.json --model 7b --branch paged-prefetch-experiments --out results/ppx
- quick plot: jq '.latencies | map(.p99)' results/ppx/summary.json | uniq -c

If this looks reasonable I'll merge the notes into the Confluence draft and open a follow-up RFC for the fused-op scheduling change.

-- Marina
